_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Mathematics unit lecture film, Halves and Wholes. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson's own order - two equal parts, colour one half, half of a group, half of a number, two halves make a whole - and use the lesson page's own numbers: the square and the strip cut near one end, six apples on two plates, eight counters in two rows, half of ten, and three wholes made of six halves. Every division drawn in this film is cut at the exact middle, except the strip that the film names as NOT equal and then repairs.
title: Halves and Wholes
subtitle: Grade 1 Mathematics
objectives: Understand that an object or shape can be split into two equal parts or two unequal parts.
Understand that a half can describe one of two equal parts of a quantity or set of objects.
Understand that a half can act as an operator (whole number answers).
Understand and visualise that halves can be combined to make wholes.

beats.say: Half means two parts, and both are exactly the same size.
Cut a shape fairly, and each part you get is one half.
Look at this square. A line goes straight down the middle.
The two parts match. Swap them over and you would not notice.
That is equal. Equal means exactly the same size, not nearly.
Now look at this strip. It is cut near one end.
One part is fat and one is thin. They are not equal.
Two parts is not enough. Both parts must be the same size.

at.both: Both parts must be the same size

beats.say: This circle is already cut into two equal parts.
Colour one part, and then stop. That piece is one half.
One of two equal parts is one half. One part, not both.
Colour both parts and you colour every bit of the circle.
That is not a half. That is the whole shape.
Half is not only for shapes. You can halve a pile of things.
Here are six apples and two plates. Do not guess.
Deal them out one at a time, like cards. Empty the pile.
Three on each plate. Both plates end up with exactly the same.
So half of six is three, and nobody is left out.
Halving a number is the same job as sharing a pile.
Take eight counters. Share them into two equal rows.
Now count one row only. One, two, three, four.
Four and four make eight, so half of eight is four.
Do not count them all. Eight is what you started with.
Halving makes a number smaller. Half of ten is five.
Here is one half of a circle. It has a straight edge.
Find the piece that fills the empty space exactly.
It has to be the same size, and the same shape.
Push the two halves together and the circle is whole again.
Every whole takes two halves. Count them: two, four, six.
Three whole oranges are made from six halves.
A half is one of two parts that are exactly the same size.
Half of a group, and half of a number, is a fair share.
And two halves always make one whole. Now it is your turn.
